title: Justinian codifies Roman law
summary: Emperor Justinian I's commission compiled centuries of Roman law into the Corpus Juris Civilis, the basis of later civil-law systems.
description: Soon after taking the throne in 527, Justinian I appointed a commission led by the jurist Tribonian to collect and harmonise Roman law. The Code appeared in 529 and in revised form in 534, the Digest of juristic writings and the Institutes textbook in 533, and his later laws were gathered as the Novels. Rediscovered in western Europe in the late 11th century and taught at Bologna, the Corpus Juris Civilis became the foundation of the civil-law tradition used across continental Europe, Latin America and beyond.

title: Volcanic winter of 536
summary: A volcanic dust veil dimmed the sun across the Northern Hemisphere in 536, beginning one of the coldest decades of the past two thousand years.
description: The Byzantine historian Procopius wrote that in 536 the sun gave light without brightness for a whole year, and Irish, Chinese and Mesopotamian sources record similar dimming, summer frosts and famine. Tree rings and Greenland and Antarctic ice cores show the cause was a large volcanic eruption, possibly in Iceland, followed by further eruptions around 540 and 547. Northern summer temperatures fell by roughly 1.5–2.5 °C, beginning a cool interval sometimes called the Late Antique Little Ice Age (c. 536–660). The source volcanoes are still debated: Ilopango in El Salvador was once proposed for the eruption of about 539–540, but volcanic glass from its Tierra Blanca Joven eruption, identified in a Greenland ice core, now dates that eruption to 431 ± 2 CE.

title: Hagia Sophia completed
summary: Justinian's great church in Constantinople, crowned by a dome about 31 m across, was consecrated after only five years of building.
description: After the Nika riots of 532 destroyed the previous church, Justinian commissioned the mathematicians Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus to design a new cathedral. Its central dome, carried on pendentives over a square bay, was a structural breakthrough, and the building remained the largest cathedral in the world for nearly a thousand years. The first dome partly collapsed after earthquakes in 558 and was rebuilt higher by 562. After the Ottoman conquest of 1453 it was converted into a mosque, and its design served as the model for the great Ottoman imperial mosques.

title: Plague of Justinian
summary: The first recorded pandemic of bubonic plague swept the Mediterranean from 541, killing a large share of Constantinople's population.
description: Plague appeared at Pelusium in Egypt in 541 and reached Constantinople in 542, where Procopius described thousands dying each day. Ancient DNA from early medieval burials in Germany, Spain and elsewhere confirms that the cause was Yersinia pestis, the bacterium later responsible for the Black Death. Outbreaks recurred around the Mediterranean and Near East for about two centuries until roughly 750. The overall death toll is debated: older estimates of 25–50 million are challenged by recent studies arguing that its demographic impact was smaller and more uneven.

title: Burning and decline of Teotihuacan
summary: The ceremonial core of Teotihuacan, once a city of perhaps 100,000 people, was burned and the city lost its dominance in central Mexico.
description: Teotihuacan was the largest city in the Americas during the first half of the first millennium CE, with an estimated population of 100,000 or more. Around the mid-6th century the temples and elite residences along the Avenue of the Dead were deliberately burned and sculptures smashed. Whether this was the work of invaders or of an internal revolt is debated, and drought and social strain may also have contributed. The city shrank but was never completely abandoned, and the Aztecs later revered its ruins as the place where the gods were born.

title: Tiwanaku at its height
summary: Near Lake Titicaca, the city of Tiwanaku led an influential Andean state built on raised-field farming and long-distance llama caravans.
description: Tiwanaku, at about 3,850 m altitude in present-day Bolivia, flourished between roughly 500 and 1000 CE, with monumental platforms such as the Akapana and the carved Gateway of the Sun. Its farmers worked raised fields around Lake Titicaca, and its influence spread through colonies and trade into southern Peru, northern Chile and eastern Bolivia. It coexisted with the Wari state to the north, with which it shared religious imagery. The polity declined around 1000–1100, possibly linked to prolonged drought, though the role of climate is debated.

title: Sui dynasty reunifies China
summary: The Sui ended nearly three centuries of division, reunified China in 589 and dug the Grand Canal linking the Yangtze to the north.
description: Yang Jian seized power in northern China in 581 as Emperor Wen of Sui and conquered the southern Chen dynasty in 589, reuniting China for the first time since the early 4th century. The Sui standardised coinage, strengthened the civil-service examinations and rebuilt the Great Wall. Under Emperor Yang (r. 604–618) huge levies of labourers built the Grand Canal, connecting the rice-growing Yangtze valley with the northern capitals. Costly failed campaigns against the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo provoked revolts, and the dynasty fell in 618, leaving its institutions to the Tang.

title: Tang dynasty
summary: From Chang'an, perhaps the largest city in the world, the Tang presided over a cosmopolitan golden age of Chinese culture.
description: Founded by Li Yuan and his son Li Shimin (Emperor Taizong), the Tang dynasty extended Chinese power deep into Central Asia and made Chang'an, with perhaps a million inhabitants, a cosmopolitan hub of the Silk Road. The era is regarded as a high point of Chinese poetry, with Li Bai and Du Fu, and saw the flourishing of Buddhism, woodblock printing and the examination system. The An Lushan Rebellion of 755–763 caused enormous loss of life and permanently weakened central authority. After decades of regional warlordism the dynasty ended in 907.

title: The Hijra: Muhammad moves to Medina
summary: Muhammad and his followers migrated from Mecca to Medina, founding the first Muslim community; the year became year 1 of the Islamic calendar.
description: According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad began receiving revelations around 610 near Mecca, but opposition from the city's Quraysh elite led him and his followers to migrate about 340 km north to Yathrib, afterwards called Medina. There he led a community that combined religious and political authority, fought and negotiated with Mecca, and took control of it in 630. By his death in 632 much of the Arabian Peninsula had accepted his leadership. Caliph Umar later made the year of the Hijra the starting point of the Islamic calendar.

title: Brahmagupta's rules for zero
summary: Indian astronomer Brahmagupta's Brahmasphutasiddhanta set out the earliest known rules for arithmetic with zero as a number, plus rules for negative numbers.
description: Written in 628 at Bhillamala (modern Bhinmal, Rajasthan), the Brahmasphutasiddhanta treats zero as a number in its own right and states rules for calculating with zero, positive 'fortunes' and negative 'debts'. It also gave methods for solving quadratic and certain indeterminate equations. Translated into Arabic in Baghdad in the 8th century, it helped carry Indian numerals and mathematics to the Islamic world and later to Europe. Some of his rules, such as those for dividing by zero, differ from modern mathematics.

title: Early Muslim conquests
summary: Under the first caliphs, Arab armies defeated Byzantium and Sasanian Persia, taking Syria, Iraq, Egypt and Iran within about 25 years.
description: After Muhammad's death in 632 the Rashidun caliphs Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali united Arabia and launched campaigns beyond it. Victories at Yarmouk and al-Qadisiyyah around 636 opened Syria and Iraq, the Sasanian capital Ctesiphon fell in 637, Egypt was taken by 642, and the last Sasanian shah, Yazdegerd III, was killed near Merv in 651. Both great empires had been exhausted by the Byzantine–Sasanian war of 602–628 and by plague. The conquests reshaped the Near East, though most conquered populations converted to Islam only gradually over the following centuries.

title: Umayyad Caliphate
summary: Ruling from Damascus, the Umayyads built an empire stretching from Iberia and Morocco to the Indus valley.
description: Muawiya I founded the Umayyad dynasty in 661 after the first Muslim civil war and made Damascus its capital. Under the Umayyads Arabic became the language of administration, a distinctive Islamic coinage was introduced, and monuments such as the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem (691–692) and the Great Mosque of Damascus were built. Expansion reached Iberia, Transoxiana and Sindh in the 710s. Resentment among non-Arab Muslims and rival factions fed the Abbasid revolution, which overthrew the dynasty in 750, though a surviving prince founded the Umayyad emirate of Córdoba.

title: Battle of Karbala
summary: Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of Muhammad, was killed by Umayyad forces at Karbala, an event central to Shia Islam and mourned each year at Ashura.
description: After the death of Caliph Muawiya, Husayn refused allegiance to his son Yazid I and set out for Kufa with a small band of relatives and supporters. They were intercepted and killed at Karbala in Iraq by a much larger Umayyad army. Husayn's death became a defining event for Shia Muslims and deepened the division with the Sunni majority over legitimate leadership of the community. It is commemorated annually on Ashura, and his shrine at Karbala is one of the holiest pilgrimage sites in Shia Islam.

title: Srivijaya rises in Sumatra
summary: From Palembang, the Buddhist maritime state of Srivijaya came to dominate shipping through the Strait of Malacca for centuries.
description: The Kedukan Bukit inscription, dated 683 and found near Palembang, records an expedition by a ruler who founded the polity known as Srivijaya; it is among the oldest surviving texts in Old Malay. The Chinese monk Yijing, who studied there in the late 7th century, described it as a major centre of Buddhist learning. By controlling the Strait of Malacca and the Sunda Strait, Srivijaya profited from trade between China, India and the Islamic world. It was weakened by the Chola raid of around 1025 and had faded by the 13th century.

title: Umayyad conquest of Hispania
summary: Berber and Arab forces under Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from North Africa in 711, defeated the Visigoths and took most of Iberia within a decade.
description: In 711 Tariq ibn Ziyad, a commander serving the Umayyad governor Musa ibn Nusayr, landed near Gibraltar, whose name derives from Jabal Tariq, 'Tariq's mountain'. He defeated and killed the Visigothic king Roderic, probably near the Guadalete river, and the Visigothic kingdom collapsed within a few years. The Muslim-ruled territory, al-Andalus, became a centre of learning and culture, especially under the Caliphate of Córdoba (929–1031). Small Christian realms survived in the north, from which the centuries-long Reconquista began.

title: Battle of Tours
summary: Frankish forces under Charles Martel defeated an Umayyad army from al-Andalus between Tours and Poitiers, killing its governor.
description: An army under Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, governor of al-Andalus, raided north into Aquitaine and was met by Charles Martel's Franks somewhere between Poitiers and Tours. The Franks held their ground, Abd al-Rahman was killed, and the Umayyad force withdrew. Later writers such as Edward Gibbon presented the battle as having saved Christian Europe, but many modern historians see it as one of a series of frontier clashes and stress the Umayyads' own internal difficulties. It greatly boosted the prestige of Charles Martel and the Carolingian family.

title: Abbasid Caliphate and the founding of Baghdad
summary: The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads and in 762 founded Baghdad, which grew into one of the largest and richest cities in the world.
description: The Abbasid revolution, launched from Khurasan in eastern Iran, defeated the Umayyads at the Battle of the Zab in 750. Caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad as a planned round city on the Tigris in 762, near the old Persian capital Ctesiphon, shifting the empire's centre of gravity eastward. Under caliphs such as Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun the court sponsored trade, scholarship and the translation of Greek, Persian and Indian works, in what is often called the Islamic Golden Age. From the 10th century real power passed to regional dynasties and military rulers, though Abbasid caliphs reigned in Baghdad until the Mongol sack of 1258.

title: Abbasids defeat the Tang at the Battle of Talas
summary: An Abbasid army defeated a Tang Chinese force near the Talas River in Central Asia after the Tang's Karluk Turkic allies changed sides.
description: In 751 a Tang army under Gao Xianzhi, a general of Korean (Goguryeo) descent, marched west across the Tian Shan and met an Abbasid force under Ziyad ibn Salih near the Talas River, in what is now Kyrgyzstan or Kazakhstan. The Tang were routed after their Karluk Turkic allies changed sides during the fighting. The defeat did not by itself end Chinese power in Central Asia; the An Lushan rebellion, which began in 755 and drew Tang troops back east, did more to bring about the Tang retreat from the region. A later tradition, recorded by the 11th-century writer al-Tha'alibi, says Chinese prisoners taken at Talas taught papermaking in Samarkand, but paper was probably already known in the region, and the craft spread into the Islamic world more gradually than the story suggests.

title: Viking raid on Lindisfarne
summary: Norse raiders sacked the island monastery of Lindisfarne in Northumbria, an attack traditionally taken as the start of the Viking Age.
description: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the destruction of the church on Lindisfarne by heathen raiders in 793, and the scholar Alcuin wrote to the Northumbrian king that nothing like it had been seen in Britain before. Scandinavian raiders in fast, shallow-draught longships went on to strike coasts and rivers across the British Isles, Francia and beyond. Over the next two centuries Norse people also traded, settled and founded polities from Dublin and the Danelaw to Normandy and the lands of the Rus'. The 793 starting date is a convention: earlier contacts are known, including a deadly clash at Portland around 789.

title: Borobudur built in Java
summary: The Shailendra dynasty raised Borobudur in central Java, the world's largest Buddhist monument, with some 2,670 carved relief panels.
description: Borobudur is a stepped stupa-mandala of nine stacked platforms, six square and three circular, crowned by a central dome and 72 perforated stupas each sheltering a Buddha statue. Its galleries carry about 2,670 relief panels illustrating Buddhist teachings and scenes of Javanese life. Construction is dated to roughly 780–830 under the Mahayana Buddhist Shailendra dynasty, which had close ties to Srivijaya. After the political centre of Java moved east in the 10th century it was neglected and partly buried by volcanic ash and vegetation until its restoration in the 19th and 20th centuries.

title: Charlemagne crowned emperor
summary: Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne emperor of the Romans in St Peter's Basilica, reviving a western empire after three centuries.
description: Charlemagne had expanded the Frankish kingdom through campaigns against the Lombards, Saxons and Avars until it covered much of western and central Europe. His coronation on Christmas Day 800 created a western imperial title that rivalled the Byzantine emperor in Constantinople. His court at Aachen sponsored the Carolingian Renaissance, which revived Latin learning, spread the Carolingian minuscule script and preserved many classical texts. His empire was divided among his grandsons by the Treaty of Verdun in 843, roughly outlining the future France and Germany.

title: Al-Khwarizmi's book on algebra
summary: In Baghdad, Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote the treatise that gave algebra its name and systematically solved linear and quadratic equations.
description: Al-Khwarizmi, a scholar at the Abbasid court of al-Ma'mun, wrote 'The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing', and its term al-jabr gave us the word algebra. It presented general methods for solving linear and quadratic equations, justified geometrically, and applied them to practical problems such as inheritance and commerce. His separate work on Hindu–Arabic numerals, known in Latin as 'Algoritmi de numero Indorum', spread decimal place-value arithmetic in Europe and is the source of the word algorithm. The exact dates of his works are uncertain; the algebra is usually placed between about 813 and 833.

title: House of Wisdom in Baghdad
summary: Under Caliph al-Ma'mun, Baghdad's House of Wisdom became a centre for translating Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic.
description: The Bayt al-Hikma began as a palace library under Harun al-Rashid and flourished under al-Ma'mun (r. 813–833). Scholars in Baghdad translated works by Aristotle, Galen, Euclid and Ptolemy, often via Syriac, along with Persian and Sanskrit texts, and produced original work in mathematics, astronomy and medicine. Historians debate how far the House of Wisdom was a formal academy rather than a library and archive within a broader translation movement funded by many patrons. That movement preserved much of Greek science, later transmitted to Europe through Latin translations.

title: Classic Maya collapse
summary: Most great Classic Maya cities of the southern lowlands, such as Tikal and Calakmul, stopped erecting monuments and were largely abandoned.
description: In the 8th and 9th centuries the dense network of Maya city-states in present-day Guatemala, Belize and southern Mexico broke down: dated stone monuments ceased, royal dynasties vanished and populations fell sharply. The last Long Count date at Tikal is from 869, and the last known anywhere is from 909 at Toniná. Proposed causes include endemic warfare, overpopulation, environmental degradation and severe droughts recorded in lake sediments and cave stalagmites. Most scholars favour a combination of factors, and cities in northern Yucatán such as Chichén Itzá continued to flourish afterwards.

title: Chaco Canyon great houses
summary: Ancestral Puebloans in New Mexico built multi-storey great houses such as Pueblo Bonito, linked by straight roads across the San Juan Basin.
description: Between about 850 and 1150 Chaco Canyon was the hub of a regional network of Ancestral Puebloan communities. Its great houses, including Pueblo Bonito with roughly 650 to 800 rooms, were planned and built over generations with timber carried from mountains some 70–80 km away, and several buildings align with solar and lunar cycles. Turquoise working and imports such as scarlet macaws and cacao from Mesoamerica show long-distance exchange. Construction stopped during a severe drought in the mid-12th century, and the population dispersed to other parts of the Southwest.

title: Cyril and Methodius' mission to the Slavs
summary: Byzantine brothers Cyril and Methodius brought a Slavonic liturgy to Great Moravia, creating the Glagolitic alphabet to write it.
description: At the request of Prince Rastislav of Great Moravia, Emperor Michael III sent the brothers Constantine (later called Cyril) and Methodius from Thessalonica in 863. They devised the Glagolitic script and translated scripture and liturgy into Old Church Slavonic, the first Slavic literary language. After their disciples were expelled from Moravia in 885, they continued their work in Bulgaria, where the Cyrillic script was developed and named in Cyril's honour. Cyrillic is now used for Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian and many other languages.

title: Diamond Sutra printed
summary: A woodblock-printed Diamond Sutra found in the Mogao Caves near Dunhuang is the oldest surviving complete printed book bearing a date.
description: The scroll, about five metres long, carries a colophon saying it was made for free distribution on behalf of a man's parents, on a date corresponding to 11 May 868. Its finely cut frontispiece shows that woodblock printing was already a mature craft in Tang China. It was sealed in a cave library at Dunhuang around 1000, acquired by Aurel Stein in 1907 and is now in the British Library. Woodblock printing had originated in East Asia by the 7th or 8th century, and older undated printed fragments survive in Korea and Japan.

title: Norse settlement of Iceland
summary: Norse settlers, traditionally led by Ingólfr Arnarson at Reykjavík, colonised Iceland and in about 930 founded the Althing assembly.
description: Medieval Icelandic sources date the first permanent settlement to about 874, and the oldest settlement remains lie just above the so-called landnám tephra, a volcanic ash layer from around 877. Settlers came from Norway and from Norse communities in Britain and Ireland, bringing enslaved Irish and Scottish people with them. By about 930 most usable land had been claimed and the Althing, a general assembly meeting at Þingvellir, was established; it is often described as one of the oldest surviving parliaments. Irish monks may have visited the island before the Norse arrived.

title: Kievan Rus' takes shape
summary: Oleg, a Varangian ruler from Novgorod, made Kyiv his capital, uniting Rus' lands along the river route from the Baltic to Byzantium.
description: According to the Primary Chronicle, Scandinavian Rus' under Rurik established themselves at Novgorod around 862, and his successor Oleg captured Kyiv in 882. The resulting state controlled the river trade from the Baltic to the Black Sea and Constantinople, exchanging furs, wax and slaves for silver and silk. In 988 Grand Prince Vladimir I accepted Orthodox Christianity from Byzantium, shaping the religion, script and art of the East Slavs. The chronicle's early dates are semi-legendary, and the relative roles of Scandinavians and Slavs in founding the state were long debated.

title: Ibn Fadlan meets the Volga Rus'
summary: Abbasid envoy Ahmad ibn Fadlan travelled to the Volga Bulgars and wrote a vivid eyewitness account of Rus' traders and a ship burial.
description: In 921 Caliph al-Muqtadir sent an embassy from Baghdad to the king of the Volga Bulgars, who had asked for religious instruction and help building a fortress. Ibn Fadlan, its secretary, recorded the customs of the Oghuz Turks, the Bulgars and especially the Rus', Scandinavian traders on the Volga. His description of a Rus' chieftain's funeral, with a ship cremation and human sacrifice, is one of the few contemporary written accounts of Viking-Age rites. His account shows the reach of Abbasid diplomacy and the fur and silver trade linking Scandinavia with the Islamic world.

title: Medieval Warm Period
summary: Relatively warm conditions around the North Atlantic coincided with Norse expansion, while other regions suffered prolonged megadroughts.
description: Tree rings, ice cores, corals and lake sediments show that many regions, especially around the North Atlantic, were relatively warm between roughly 950 and 1250. These conditions coincided with Norse settlement of Greenland and with expanding agriculture in Europe. Warmth was not synchronous worldwide, however, and parts of the Americas experienced severe megadroughts that may have stressed societies such as Chaco Canyon. Reconstructions indicate that global average temperatures were lower than those of the late 20th and 21st centuries, and scientists increasingly prefer the term Medieval Climate Anomaly.

title: Song dynasty
summary: The Song reunified most of China and oversaw a commercial and technological boom including paper money, gunpowder weapons, movable type and the compass.
description: Zhao Kuangyin founded the Song in 960 with its capital at Kaifeng. Rice cultivation in the south, expanding markets and the first government-issued paper money (1024) supported a population that may have exceeded 100 million. Civil-service examinations produced a scholar-official elite, and Neo-Confucian philosophy took shape. After the Jurchen Jin captured Kaifeng in 1127 the court moved south to Hangzhou as the Southern Song, which finally fell to the Mongols in 1279.

title: Otto I crowned emperor
summary: German king Otto I, victor over the Magyars at Lechfeld, was crowned emperor in Rome, beginning what was later called the Holy Roman Empire.
description: Otto I had strengthened royal power in Germany and in 955 decisively defeated the Magyars at the Battle of Lechfeld near Augsburg, ending their raids into western Europe. His coronation by Pope John XII on 2 February 962 tied the imperial title to the German kingship for the rest of the Middle Ages. The realm, later called the Holy Roman Empire, persisted in changing forms until 1806. Some historians instead date the empire's beginning to Charlemagne's coronation in 800.

title: Fatimids conquer Egypt and found Cairo
summary: The Shi'a Fatimid caliphs, rivals of the Abbasids, conquered Egypt and built a new capital, Cairo, which grew into a great centre of trade and learning.
description: The Fatimids, an Isma'ili Shi'a dynasty claiming descent from Muhammad's daughter Fatima, proclaimed a rival caliphate in Ifriqiya (modern Tunisia) in 909, challenging the Sunni Abbasids. In 969 their general Jawhar al-Siqilli conquered Egypt and laid out a walled palace city beside the older capital Fustat, which became known as al-Qahira, 'the Victorious'; Caliph al-Mu'izz moved there in 973. The al-Azhar mosque, begun in 970, became a leading centre of learning and is often described as one of the world's oldest continuously operating universities. At their height the Fatimids ruled North Africa, Egypt, Sicily, parts of the Levant and the Hejaz, and Cairo prospered on Mediterranean and Red Sea trade. The dynasty declined in the 12th century and was abolished in 1171 by Saladin, who restored allegiance to the Abbasid caliph.

title: The Tale of Genji
summary: Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting at the Heian court in Kyoto, wrote The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel.
description: The Heian period (794–1185), named after the capital Heian-kyō (Kyoto), saw a flowering of court culture in which women writing in the kana syllabary produced much of the finest literature. Murasaki Shikibu's 54-chapter tale follows the life and loves of the 'shining prince' Genji and his descendants with psychological depth and close attention to court aesthetics. Its exact date is uncertain, but her diary shows parts were circulating by 1008. Whether it is the 'first novel' depends on definitions, but it remains a central classic of Japanese literature.

title: Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics
summary: Working in Cairo, Ibn al-Haytham argued that vision results from light entering the eye and tested optical claims through controlled experiments.
description: The seven-volume Kitab al-Manazir rejected the ancient theory that the eye emits rays and argued instead that light from objects enters the eye. Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) investigated reflection, refraction and the camera obscura, combining mathematics with systematic experiment. Translated into Latin around 1200, it influenced European scholars such as Roger Bacon and Johannes Kepler. Tradition says he wrote it in Fatimid Cairo while feigning madness to escape the caliph al-Hakim, though this story may be legendary.

title: Norse in Newfoundland: L'Anse aux Meadows
summary: Norse Greenlanders built a camp in Newfoundland, the only confirmed pre-Columbian Norse site in the Americas outside Greenland; wood was cut there in 1021.
description: Icelandic sagas describe voyages to 'Vinland' by Leif Erikson around 1000, setting out from the Greenland colony founded by his father Erik the Red in about 985. In 1960 Helge Ingstad and Anne Stine Ingstad identified Norse buildings at L'Anse aux Meadows, with iron-working debris and Norse artefacts. In 2021 researchers used the radiocarbon spike from a cosmic-ray event in 993 to show that wood there was cut with metal tools in 1021. The site was occupied only briefly, and the Norse made no lasting settlement in North America beyond Greenland.

title: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine
summary: Persian polymath Ibn Sina (Avicenna) completed the Canon of Medicine, a medical encyclopedia taught in Islamic and European schools for six centuries.
description: Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037) served as physician and vizier to rulers in Iran and wrote some 200 works on philosophy, science and medicine. His five-book al-Qanun fi al-Tibb synthesised Greek medicine, especially Galen, with Persian and Indian knowledge and his own clinical observations, and discussed contagion, quarantine and the testing of drugs. Translated into Latin by Gerard of Cremona in the 12th century, it remained a standard textbook in European medical schools into the 17th century. His philosophical Book of Healing deeply influenced both Islamic and Latin scholastic thought.

title: Chola naval raid on Srivijaya
summary: Rajendra I of the Chola dynasty sent a fleet across the Bay of Bengal to sack ports of Srivijaya in Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula.
description: Under Rajaraja I (r. 985–1014) and his son Rajendra I (r. 1014–1044), the Tamil Chola dynasty of southern India built a powerful navy and an empire reaching Sri Lanka and the Maldives; Rajaraja's Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur was completed in 1010. Around 1025 a Chola fleet attacked Srivijaya's ports, including Kadaram (Kedah) and Palembang, and captured its king, according to Rajendra's inscriptions. The raid probably aimed to secure the trade route to China rather than to hold territory. It weakened Srivijaya's control of the straits.

title: Earliest written gunpowder formulas
summary: The Song military manual Wujing Zongyao gave the first known recipes for gunpowder, used in fire arrows, incendiary bombs and smoke weapons.
description: Chinese alchemists had discovered the incendiary properties of mixtures of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal by the 9th century, apparently while seeking elixirs. The Wujing Zongyao, compiled for the Song court and completed in 1044, records several gunpowder formulas and describes fire arrows and grenade-like bombs. Over the following centuries the Song, Jin and Mongols developed fire lances, explosive bombs and the first guns; the oldest surviving metal guns date from the late 13th century. Knowledge of gunpowder reached the Islamic world and Europe in the 13th century and eventually transformed warfare worldwide.

title: Bi Sheng invents movable type
summary: A commoner named Bi Sheng made the first known movable type from fired clay characters, as described by the scholar Shen Kuo.
description: Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays (c. 1088) relate that during the Qingli era (1041–1048) Bi Sheng carved individual characters in clay, hardened them by fire and set them in an iron frame bedded with resin and wax for printing. The method suited large print runs but was less convenient than carved woodblocks for a script with thousands of characters, so woodblock printing remained dominant in China. Wooden type was later used, notably by Wang Zhen around 1300, and cast metal type was developed in Korea. Almost nothing is known about Bi Sheng beyond Shen Kuo's account.

title: Cahokia, city of the Mississippians
summary: Near modern St Louis, Cahokia grew into the largest pre-Columbian settlement north of Mexico, centred on the 30 m high Monks Mound.
description: Around 1050 Cahokia underwent a rapid burst of planned construction, with plazas, about 120 earthen mounds and a population estimated at 10,000–20,000 at its peak. Monks Mound, the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas, covers about 6 hectares at its base. Cahokia was the political and religious centre of the Mississippian culture, whose influence spread across the Midwest and Southeast. The city declined after about 1200 and was largely abandoned by around 1350–1400; floods, drought, warfare and political fragmentation have all been proposed as causes.

title: East–West Schism
summary: Papal legates excommunicated Patriarch Michael Cerularius at Hagia Sophia, a rupture that came to symbolise the split of Catholic and Orthodox churches.
description: Long-standing disputes over papal authority, the Filioque clause in the Creed, the use of unleavened bread and other practices came to a head in 1054. Cardinal Humbert placed a bull excommunicating the patriarch on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and the patriarch's synod excommunicated the legates in return. Historians stress that the separation was gradual: contacts continued, and the sack of Constantinople by the Fourth Crusade in 1204 did more to harden the division. The mutual excommunications were lifted in 1965, but the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches remain separate.

title: Battle of Hastings
summary: William, Duke of Normandy, defeated and killed King Harold II of England, beginning the Norman conquest of England.
description: Harold Godwinson was crowned in January 1066, but both William of Normandy and Harald Hardrada of Norway claimed the throne. Harold defeated Hardrada at Stamford Bridge near York on 25 September, then marched south to face William, who had landed at Pevensey. After a day-long battle Harold was killed and English resistance crumbled; William was crowned on Christmas Day. The conquest replaced the English aristocracy with a French-speaking Norman elite, reshaped the English language and led to the Domesday survey of 1086.

title: Al-Bakri describes the Ghana Empire
summary: Andalusian geographer al-Bakri described the gold-rich West African kingdom of Ghana and its twin-town capital, probably Koumbi Saleh.
description: The Ghana (Wagadu) Empire of the Soninke people, in the Sahel of present-day southern Mauritania and western Mali, grew rich by controlling the trans-Saharan trade in gold from the upper Senegal and Niger rivers in exchange for salt and North African goods. Writing in Córdoba in 1068 from merchants' reports, al-Bakri described a royal town and a separate Muslim merchants' town with twelve mosques. The capital is usually identified with the excavated site of Koumbi Saleh. Ghana's origins probably lie centuries earlier, and it declined in the 12th and 13th centuries; the extent of an Almoravid conquest around 1076 is debated.

title: Battle of Manzikert
summary: The Seljuk Turks under Sultan Alp Arslan defeated and captured Byzantine Emperor Romanos IV, opening Anatolia to Turkish settlement.
description: The Seljuks, Turkic nomads who had converted to Islam, took Baghdad in 1055 and became protectors of the Abbasid caliph. At Manzikert (Malazgirt) in eastern Anatolia, Alp Arslan defeated a Byzantine army weakened by desertion and took Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes prisoner. The defeat itself was not catastrophic, but the Byzantine civil wars that followed allowed Turkish groups to occupy much of Anatolia. Byzantine appeals for western help contributed to the launch of the First Crusade in 1095.

title: Shen Kuo describes the magnetic compass
summary: Song scholar Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays gave the first clear description of a magnetised needle compass and of magnetic declination.
description: Shen Kuo (1031–1095), a statesman and polymath, wrote the Dream Pool Essays in retirement at his garden estate in Zhenjiang. He described needles magnetised by rubbing on lodestone and suspended or floated so that they point south, and noted that they deviate slightly from true north. Chinese sources record the compass in use for navigation at sea by around 1111–1117. The magnetic compass appears in European and Islamic sources around 1190–1230, though whether it spread from China or was developed independently is uncertain.

title: University of Bologna founded
summary: Students gathering to study Roman law in Bologna formed what is regarded as the oldest university in continuous operation.
description: Teachers such as Irnerius revived the study of Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis in Bologna in the late 11th century, attracting students from across Europe. The students organised themselves into nations and guilds that hired and regulated their masters; the word universitas originally meant such a corporate body. Emperor Frederick Barbarossa granted travelling scholars legal protection in 1158. The founding date of 1088 was fixed retrospectively by a committee in the 1880s, and universities at Paris, Oxford and elsewhere followed in the 12th and 13th centuries.

title: First Crusade captures Jerusalem
summary: Answering Pope Urban II's call, armies from western Europe marched to the Levant and took Jerusalem in 1099, massacring many of its inhabitants.
description: At the Council of Clermont in 1095 Urban II responded to a Byzantine request for help against the Seljuks by urging an armed pilgrimage to recover Jerusalem. After taking Nicaea and, following a long siege, Antioch, the crusaders stormed Jerusalem on 15 July 1099 and killed many of its Muslim and Jewish residents. They founded the Kingdom of Jerusalem and other crusader states, which survived in shrinking form until the fall of Acre in 1291. The crusading movement also unleashed massacres of Jewish communities in the Rhineland in 1096.

title: Polynesians settle Hawaii
summary: Voyaging canoes from central East Polynesia, probably the Society or Marquesas Islands, reached Hawaii, the most isolated archipelago on Earth.
description: Polynesian navigators sailed double-hulled canoes thousands of kilometres using stars, ocean swells and birds to find new islands. Refined radiocarbon dating of short-lived plant remains suggests that East Polynesia was settled in a rapid burst, with Hawaii colonised roughly 1000–1200, later than earlier estimates of 300–800. Settlers brought taro, breadfruit, pigs, dogs and chickens, and Hawaiian society developed into competing chiefdoms with large irrigation systems and fishponds. The exact date of first arrival remains debated.

title: Great Zimbabwe
summary: Shona ancestors built the stone city of Great Zimbabwe, capital of a kingdom that traded gold and ivory with the Swahili coast.
description: Great Zimbabwe's dry-stone walls, built without mortar, include the Great Enclosure, whose outer wall is up to 11 m high and about 250 m long, the largest ancient structure south of the Sahara. At its height in the 13th–15th centuries the city may have housed 10,000–18,000 people. Its rulers grew wealthy from cattle and from exporting gold and ivory via coastal towns such as Kilwa, as finds of Chinese porcelain and Persian glass show. Colonial-era writers falsely attributed the site to outsiders, but archaeology firmly established that it was built by Bantu-speaking ancestors of the Shona.

title: Swahili city-states flourish
summary: Trading towns such as Kilwa, Mombasa and Mogadishu linked East Africa's gold and ivory to markets across the Indian Ocean.
description: Along the East African coast from Somalia to Mozambique, African communities developed stone-built Muslim towns whose Bantu language, Swahili, absorbed many Arabic words. Ruled by local sultans, towns such as Kilwa Kisiwani grew rich by shipping gold from the Zimbabwe plateau, ivory and other goods to Arabia, Persia, India and China on the monsoon winds. Kilwa minted its own coins and built the Great Mosque and the Husuni Kubwa palace, and Ibn Battuta praised it as a beautiful city when he visited in 1331. Portuguese attacks after 1500 disrupted the trading network.

title: Angkor Wat built
summary: Khmer king Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world, at the heart of the city of Angkor.
description: The Khmer Empire, dated from Jayavarman II's proclamation as universal monarch in 802, ruled much of mainland Southeast Asia from Angkor. Angkor Wat was built as a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu, its five towers representing Mount Meru, and its galleries carry hundreds of metres of bas-reliefs. Greater Angkor, supported by an extensive network of reservoirs and canals revealed by lidar surveys, was among the largest preindustrial urban complexes in the world. The temple later became Buddhist and was never fully abandoned, though the Khmer capital moved south after the 15th century.

title: Gothic architecture begins at Saint-Denis
summary: Abbot Suger's new choir at Saint-Denis near Paris combined pointed arches, rib vaults and large stained-glass windows in the first Gothic design.
description: Suger rebuilt the royal abbey church of Saint-Denis with a choir consecrated in 1144, using pointed arches and ribbed vaults to open the walls for windows filled with coloured light. The new style spread rapidly through northern France in cathedrals such as Notre-Dame de Paris (begun 1163), Chartres and Reims, aided by the flying buttress. Gothic building demanded large, coordinated workforces and drew on the growing wealth of towns. The style dominated much of European architecture until the 16th century.

title: Nan Madol built in Micronesia
summary: On artificial islets off Pohnpei, the Saudeleur dynasty built Nan Madol from basalt columns as the seat of a centralised Micronesian state.
description: Nan Madol consists of nearly 100 artificial islets separated by tidal canals, built of stacked columnar basalt filled with coral rubble, with some walls rising over 7 m. Dating suggests megalithic construction began around 1180–1200, and the Saudeleur dynasty, which unified Pohnpei, ruled from Nan Madol until about 1628, when oral tradition says it was overthrown by the culture hero Isokelekel. The site served as royal residence, ceremonial centre and burial place. How the multi-tonne basalt columns were transported remains uncertain.

title: Kamakura shogunate
summary: After the Genpei War, Minamoto no Yoritomo set up a warrior government at Kamakura, beginning nearly 700 years of samurai rule in Japan.
description: The Minamoto clan destroyed the Taira at the naval battle of Dan-no-ura in 1185, and Yoritomo appointed military governors and land stewards across Japan; the emperor granted him the title of shogun in 1192. Real power soon passed to the Hōjō family, ruling as regents. The Kamakura period saw the spread of Pure Land, Nichiren and Zen Buddhism. The strain of repelling the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281 contributed to the shogunate's overthrow in 1333.

title: Saladin wins at Hattin and retakes Jerusalem
summary: Saladin destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem at the Horns of Hattin and retook Jerusalem three months later.
description: Saladin, a Kurdish commander, united Egypt and Syria under his Ayyubid rule and then turned on the crusader states. On 4 July 1187 he trapped the thirsty crusader army near the Sea of Galilee, capturing King Guy of Lusignan and the relic of the True Cross. Jerusalem surrendered on 2 October 1187 on negotiated terms, in contrast to the massacre of 1099. The loss prompted the Third Crusade under Richard I of England and others, which recovered coastal cities but not Jerusalem.

title: Rock-hewn churches of Lalibela
summary: In the Ethiopian highlands, eleven monolithic churches were carved downward into solid rock, traditionally under King Gebre Mesqel Lalibela.
description: Tradition credits the Zagwe king Lalibela (r. c. 1181–1221) with creating a 'New Jerusalem' at a time when pilgrimage to the Holy Land had become difficult. The churches, such as the cross-shaped Bete Giyorgis, were excavated from the top down out of volcanic rock and connected by trenches and tunnels. Archaeologists think some may have been carved earlier and modified over several centuries. Lalibela remains an active centre of Ethiopian Orthodox pilgrimage and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Polynesians settle Rapa Nui
summary: Polynesian voyagers reached remote Rapa Nui (Easter Island), where they later carved nearly a thousand monumental moai statues.
description: Radiocarbon dating suggests the island was settled around 1150–1250, among the last places reached in the Polynesian expansion. Islanders carved close to 1,000 moai from volcanic tuff at the Rano Raraku quarry and moved many of them, probably upright by 'walking' them with ropes, to stone platforms around the coast. The island was deforested, and older accounts blamed a self-inflicted ecological collapse; more recent studies argue that the population stayed relatively stable until European contact from 1722 brought disease and slave raids. That debate is ongoing.

title: Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople
summary: Crusaders bound for the Holy Land instead stormed and looted Constantinople, founding a Latin Empire and deepening the rift between Catholics and Orthodox.
description: Called by Pope Innocent III to recover Jerusalem by way of Egypt, the crusade fell deeply into debt to Venice, which had built its fleet. The crusaders first helped Venice take the Christian city of Zara (Zadar) in 1202, then sailed to Constantinople to restore the deposed emperor Isaac II and his son Alexios IV, who promised them large payments. When the money did not materialise and Alexios IV was overthrown and murdered, the crusaders stormed the city in April 1204 and plundered it for three days, carrying off treasures and relics, including the bronze horses now at St Mark's in Venice. They founded a Latin Empire and shared out Byzantine lands with Venice, while Greek successor states survived at Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond. Nicaea retook Constantinople in 1261, but the restored empire never regained its former strength.

title: Temüjin proclaimed Genghis Khan
summary: An assembly on the Onon River proclaimed Temüjin ruler of the Mongols, founding the largest contiguous land empire in history.
description: Temüjin united the feuding Mongol and Turkic tribes of the steppe through alliances and war, reorganising them into decimal military units loyal to him rather than to their clans. As Genghis Khan he attacked the Western Xia and the Jin dynasty and, from 1219, destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia with enormous loss of life. After his death in 1227 his successors conquered northern China, the Rus' principalities, Iran and Iraq, and by 1279 Mongol-ruled lands, by then divided among rival khanates, stretched from Korea to eastern Europe. Mongol rule fostered trade and exchange along the Silk Roads, but at the cost of devastation in many conquered regions.

title: Delhi Sultanate
summary: Former slave-soldier Qutb ud-Din Aibak founded a Muslim sultanate at Delhi that dominated much of northern India for three centuries.
description: Following the conquests of Muhammad of Ghor, his general Qutb ud-Din Aibak became the first sultan of Delhi in 1206 and began building the Qutb Minar. Five successive dynasties, including the Khaljis and Tughluqs, ruled from Delhi; Alauddin Khalji repelled repeated Mongol invasions, and under Muhammad bin Tughluq the sultanate reached its greatest extent in the 1330s. Its rule brought Persianate culture and Indo-Islamic architecture, and also the destruction of many Hindu, Buddhist and Jain institutions. Weakened by Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398, it ended when Babur defeated the last Lodi sultan at Panipat in 1526.

title: Magna Carta sealed
summary: Rebel barons forced King John of England to seal Magna Carta at Runnymede, establishing that the king was subject to the law.
description: Heavy taxation and military failure in France led England's barons to rebel against King John in 1215. The charter agreed at Runnymede promised protection of church rights, limits on feudal payments and access to justice, including the principle that no free man could be punished except by the lawful judgement of his peers or the law of the land. John repudiated it within weeks and Pope Innocent III annulled it, but it was reissued in revised forms in 1216, 1217 and 1225. Later generations reinterpreted it as a foundation of constitutional government, influencing the English Bill of Rights and the United States Constitution.

title: Sundiata founds the Mali Empire
summary: Sundiata Keita defeated the Sosso king Sumanguru at the Battle of Kirina, founding the Mali Empire on the upper Niger.
description: The story of Sundiata, the 'lion king' of the Mandinka, is preserved in oral epics performed by griots as well as in Arabic sources. After his victory at Kirina around 1235, Mali absorbed the former lands of Ghana and controlled the gold fields of Bambuk and Bure. At its height in the 14th century it stretched from the Atlantic coast to beyond the Niger bend and included Timbuktu and Gao. The location of its capital, possibly Niani, remains uncertain, and Mali declined in the 15th century as Songhai rose.

title: Mongols sack Baghdad
summary: A Mongol army under Hülegü captured and sacked Baghdad, executed the last Abbasid caliph and ended the city's era as capital of the Islamic world.
description: Hülegü, a grandson of Genghis Khan, besieged Baghdad in January 1258, and Caliph al-Musta'sim surrendered on 10 February. The Mongols sacked the city for about a week, killing tens of thousands or more of its inhabitants; contemporary figures of 200,000 to a million dead are probably exaggerated. Libraries, including collections associated with the House of Wisdom, were destroyed, and the caliph was executed. The sack is often taken as the symbolic end of the Islamic Golden Age, although scholarship continued elsewhere, including at Hülegü's own observatory at Maragheh.

title: Battle of Ain Jalut
summary: The Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt defeated a Mongol army in Galilee, halting the Mongol advance towards Egypt and North Africa.
description: After the fall of Baghdad and Aleppo, Hülegü withdrew most of his army east on the death of the Great Khan Möngke, leaving a smaller force under Kitbuqa. The Mamluks, a ruling elite of former slave soldiers who had seized power in Egypt in 1250, met it at Ain Jalut under Sultan Qutuz and the commander Baybars. Kitbuqa was killed and the Mongols lost Syria. The victory secured Mamluk rule over Egypt and Syria until 1517 and preserved Cairo as a leading centre of Islamic learning.

title: Aquinas writes the Summa Theologiae
summary: Dominican friar Thomas Aquinas wrote his Summa Theologiae, a vast synthesis of Christian theology and Aristotelian philosophy.
description: Aquinas (c. 1225–1274), a Dominican who taught at the University of Paris and in Italy, aimed to show that faith and reason are compatible. Drawing on newly available Latin translations of Aristotle and on Muslim and Jewish thinkers such as Averroes and Maimonides, he organised the Summa as questions, objections and replies, including his 'five ways' of arguing for God's existence. He left it unfinished at his death in 1274. Thomism later became central to Catholic theology and remains influential in philosophy.

title: Kublai Khan founds the Yuan dynasty
summary: Kublai Khan proclaimed the Yuan dynasty and ruled from Dadu (Beijing); by 1279 the Mongols had conquered the Southern Song and held all of China.
description: Kublai, a grandson of Genghis Khan, won a succession war against his brother Ariq Böke (1260–1264) and in 1271 adopted the Chinese dynastic name Yuan, ruling from a new capital, Dadu (Khanbaliq), on the site of modern Beijing. His armies took the Song stronghold of Xiangyang in 1273 after a five-year siege and the capital Hangzhou in 1276, and the last Song loyalists were destroyed in a naval battle off Yamen in 1279. The Yuan was the first non-Han dynasty to rule all of China; it extended the Grand Canal to the north, relied heavily on paper currency and employed many foreign officials and merchants, while generally placing Mongols and Central Asians above Chinese subjects. Failed invasions of Japan and Southeast Asia, inflation, Yellow River floods and succession struggles weakened it, and in 1368 the last Yuan emperor fled Dadu ahead of the advancing army of the newly proclaimed Ming dynasty.

title: Marco Polo's travels to China
summary: Venetian merchant Marco Polo travelled to the court of Kublai Khan, and his account of Asia shaped European geographical imagination.
description: Marco Polo set out with his father and uncle in 1271, reaching Kublai Khan's summer capital Shangdu around 1275, and by his own account served the Yuan court for some 17 years before returning to Venice by sea in 1295. While a prisoner of war in Genoa he dictated his story to the romance writer Rustichello da Pisa. The book described Chinese cities, paper money and the burning of coal, and Christopher Columbus owned an annotated copy. Some scholars have questioned whether Polo reached China because he omits the Great Wall and tea, but most accept his account as broadly authentic.

title: Mongol invasions of Japan
summary: Kublai Khan's fleets twice attacked Japan at Hakata Bay; both invasions failed, the second after a typhoon wrecked much of the fleet.
description: Having subdued Goryeo Korea and much of China, Kublai Khan, founder of the Yuan dynasty, demanded Japan's submission. A Mongol–Korean force landed at Hakata Bay in Kyushu in 1274 but withdrew after brief fighting, and in 1281 a much larger fleet, including former Southern Song ships, was held off by coastal walls and samurai before a typhoon destroyed it. The storms became known as kamikaze, 'divine winds'. Underwater archaeology off Takashima has found remains of the 1281 fleet, including evidence of hastily built ships.

title: Polynesians settle New Zealand
summary: Voyagers from East Polynesia reached Aotearoa New Zealand, the last large habitable landmass on Earth to be settled by humans.
description: Radiocarbon dates, and the appearance of the first human impacts on forests shortly before the Kaharoa eruption of about 1314, indicate that ancestors of the Māori arrived around 1250–1300, probably in several waves of voyaging canoes. Early sites such as Wairau Bar contain East Polynesian artefacts and abundant moa bones. Within about two centuries hunting and forest clearance had driven all nine species of moa and other large birds extinct. Māori culture developed distinctively as people adapted to a temperate climate, including fortified pā settlements.

title: Osman I founds the Ottoman state
summary: Osman, leader of a small Turkish principality in north-west Anatolia, founded the dynasty that would build the Ottoman Empire.
description: As the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum fragmented under Mongol domination, Turkish frontier lords competed for land on the Byzantine border. Osman's principality around Söğüt expanded at Byzantine expense, and his son Orhan took Bursa in 1326 and made it the capital. The Ottomans crossed into Europe in the 1350s, fought a Serbian-led coalition at Kosovo in 1389 in a battle that killed both commanders but left Serbia a vassal, survived defeat by Timur in 1402 and took Constantinople in 1453. The traditional founding date of 1299 is symbolic, and little about Osman's early career is certain.

title: Onset of the Little Ice Age
summary: Cooling set in after a cluster of large volcanic eruptions, beginning a colder period that lasted until the 19th century.
description: From around 1300 glaciers advanced in the Alps and elsewhere, and northern summers became cooler and more variable. Ice cores and tree rings point to a sequence of large eruptions, including the 1257 Samalas eruption on Lombok in Indonesia, one of the largest of the past two thousand years, along with periods of low solar activity. Cold, wet years contributed to the Great Famine of 1315–1317 in northern Europe and to the abandonment of the Norse settlements in Greenland. The start date is debated, with proposals ranging from about 1250 to 1550, and the coldest phases came in the 17th century.

title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca
summary: Mali's ruler Mansa Musa travelled to Mecca with a vast caravan, spending and giving away so much gold in Cairo that its value there fell for years.
description: Mansa Musa (r. c. 1312–1337) ruled the Mali Empire at its height, when it supplied a large share of the gold traded across the Sahara. On his hajj he passed through Cairo with thousands of attendants and camels carrying gold, and the chronicler al-Umari reported that his generosity depressed the price of gold in Egypt for years. The journey made Mali famous as far as Europe: the Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows him holding a gold nugget. He returned with scholars and the architect al-Sahili, associated with the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu, which became a renowned centre of Islamic learning.

title: Founding of Tenochtitlan
summary: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, which grew into the Aztec capital and one of the largest cities in the world.
description: According to Mexica tradition, the migrants saw their prophesied sign of an eagle perched on a cactus on a marshy island and founded their city there in 1325. With causeways, aqueducts and chinampa farm plots, Tenochtitlan grew to perhaps 200,000 inhabitants by 1519, dominated by the twin temples of the Templo Mayor. In 1428 it formed the Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan, which built the Aztec Empire through conquest and tribute across central Mexico. The city fell to Spanish and allied Indigenous forces in 1521, and Mexico City was built on its ruins.

title: Ibn Battuta's travels
summary: Moroccan scholar Ibn Battuta set out from Tangier on a pilgrimage and travelled for nearly 30 years, from West Africa to China.
description: Leaving Tangier in 1325, Ibn Battuta visited Mecca, Persia, Anatolia, the Swahili coast, the Golden Horde, India, where he served the Delhi sultan as a judge, the Maldives, Southeast Asia and probably China, and later crossed the Sahara to the Mali Empire. On his return he dictated the account known as the Rihla to the writer Ibn Juzayy in Fez. His journeys, often estimated at around 120,000 km, make the Rihla a rich source on the 14th-century Islamic world. Scholars think some passages, particularly on China and the Volga, were embellished or borrowed from other writers.

title: Hundred Years' War
summary: The English and French crowns fought a long series of wars over the succession to France, ending with the English expelled from almost all of France.
description: Edward III of England claimed the French throne through his mother, starting a conflict fought intermittently from 1337 to 1453. English longbowmen won famous victories at Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415), and in 1420 the Treaty of Troyes made Henry V heir to France. A French recovery inspired by Joan of Arc and supported by improved artillery drove the English out, leaving them only Calais after the Battle of Castillon in 1453. The wars strengthened royal taxation and standing armies and fostered national identity in both countries.

title: Black Death
summary: Bubonic plague spread from the Black Sea across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, killing perhaps a third to a half of Europe's population.
description: Ancient DNA from cemeteries in present-day Kyrgyzstan dated to 1338–1339 points to an origin of the outbreak in Central Asia. The disease reached Caffa in Crimea during a siege by the Golden Horde in 1346 and was carried on Genoese ships to Constantinople, Sicily and other Mediterranean ports in 1347, spreading across Europe by 1351. Estimates suggest 25–50 million deaths in Europe and many millions more in the Middle East and North Africa. The resulting labour shortage raised wages and weakened serfdom in western Europe, while the crisis also fuelled massacres of Jewish communities. Plague returned in waves for more than three centuries.

title: Ming dynasty founded
summary: Rebel leader Zhu Yuanzhang drove the Mongol Yuan from China and founded the Ming dynasty, with its first capital at Nanjing.
description: Famine, floods and the Red Turban rebellions undermined Yuan rule, and Zhu Yuanzhang, a former peasant and Buddhist monk, emerged victorious and proclaimed himself the Hongwu Emperor in 1368. The Ming restored Han Chinese rule, rebuilt much of the Great Wall in its familiar brick-faced form and expanded agriculture and population. The Yongle Emperor moved the capital to Beijing, where the Forbidden City was completed in 1420, and sponsored Zheng He's voyages. The dynasty ruled China until 1644.

title: Conquests of Timur
summary: From Samarkand, the Turco-Mongol conqueror Timur campaigned from Anatolia to Delhi, sacking cities and causing enormous loss of life.
description: Timur (Tamerlane) seized power in Transoxiana in 1370 and spent 35 years campaigning, sacking cities including Isfahan, Baghdad, Damascus and Delhi (1398), often with massacres. In 1402 he defeated and captured the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I at Ankara, temporarily halting Ottoman expansion. He used the wealth and craftsmen seized in his conquests to adorn Samarkand with monumental buildings. He died in 1405 while preparing to invade Ming China; his descendants, the Timurids, presided over a cultural flowering, and one of them, Babur, founded the Mughal Empire.

title: Jikji printed with metal type
summary: A Buddhist text printed at Heungdeok Temple in Goryeo Korea is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type.
description: Craftsmen of the Goryeo dynasty (918–1392) were casting bronze movable type by the early 13th century; records mention a ritual text printed with metal type around 1234, but no copy survives. The Jikji, an anthology of Seon (Zen) Buddhist teachings, was printed at Heungdeoksa near Cheongju in 1377, some 78 years before Gutenberg's Bible. Only its second volume survives, held by the National Library of France. The later Joseon kings greatly expanded state printing with metal type, though woodblocks remained common.

title: Kingdom of Kongo
summary: The Kingdom of Kongo emerged south of the Congo River estuary, centred on its capital Mbanza Kongo in present-day northern Angola.
description: According to oral tradition, Lukeni lua Nimi founded the kingdom by conquest in the late 14th century, and it grew into a centralised state with provinces, taxation and a currency of nzimbu shells. The Portuguese navigator Diogo Cão reached the Congo estuary in 1483, and King Nzinga a Nkuwu was baptised as João I in 1491. His son Afonso I promoted Christianity and literacy, but the Atlantic slave trade soon destabilised the kingdom. The early chronology rests largely on oral traditions recorded later.

title: Zheng He's treasure voyages
summary: Ming admiral Zheng He led seven great fleets across the Indian Ocean, reaching Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa.
description: Commissioned by the Yongle Emperor, Zheng He, a Muslim eunuch of the imperial court, commanded fleets of up to several hundred ships and some 27,000 men. They visited Champa, Java, Malacca, Sri Lanka, Calicut, Hormuz, Aden and the Swahili coast as far as Malindi, collecting tribute and exotic goods, including a giraffe. The size of the largest 'treasure ships' given in later Ming sources, about 120 m long, is doubted by many historians and naval architects. After 1433 the court ended the voyages and later restricted private overseas trade.

title: Last record of Norse Greenland
summary: A wedding at Hvalsey Church in 1408 is the last written record of the Norse colony in Greenland, abandoned within a few decades.
description: Norse settlers led by Erik the Red founded farms in south-west Greenland around 985, and at its peak the colony may have numbered about 2,000–3,000 people. The Western Settlement was abandoned by the mid-14th century, and the Eastern Settlement disappears from records after a wedding at Hvalsey Church in 1408, reported in Iceland. Explanations include Little Ice Age cooling, falling European demand for walrus ivory, isolation from Norway and competition with Thule Inuit. Archaeology shows the settlers relied increasingly on seals, and the end may have come through gradual emigration rather than sudden collapse.

title: Joan of Arc lifts the siege of Orléans
summary: A peasant girl claiming divine guidance, Joan of Arc helped relieve the English siege of Orléans, reviving French fortunes in the Hundred Years' War.
description: Joan, from Domrémy in north-eastern France, persuaded the uncrowned Charles VII to let her accompany a relief army to Orléans, besieged by the English since October 1428. The siege was lifted within nine days of her arrival, and she escorted Charles to his coronation at Reims in July 1429. Captured by Burgundian forces in 1430 and handed to the English, she was tried for heresy and burned at Rouen on 30 May 1431. A retrial annulled the verdict in 1456, and she was canonised in 1920.

title: Brunelleschi's dome crowns Florence
summary: Filippo Brunelleschi completed the vast dome of Florence Cathedral without traditional centring, a symbol of the early Italian Renaissance.
description: Florence, enriched by banking and the wool trade and patronised by families such as the Medici, became the leading centre of a revival of classical learning and art in the 15th century. Brunelleschi's double-shelled dome, built from 1420 to 1436 with herringbone brickwork and specially designed hoisting machines, remains the largest masonry dome ever built. He is also credited with demonstrating linear perspective, soon adopted by painters such as Masaccio. Together with humanist scholarship reviving ancient texts, such work marks the early Renaissance.

title: Inca expansion under Pachacuti
summary: From Cusco, the Inca ruler Pachacuti began a rapid expansion that created Tawantinsuyu, the largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas.
description: After repelling the Chanka around 1438, Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui rebuilt Cusco and began conquests continued by his son Topa Inca and grandson Huayna Capac. At its height around 1525 the empire ran some 4,000 km along the Andes from southern Colombia to central Chile, linked by roughly 40,000 km of roads, and ruled perhaps 10 million people. It functioned without markets or alphabetic writing, relying on labour tribute (mit'a), state storehouses and knotted-cord khipu records; royal estates such as Machu Picchu date from this period. Pachacuti's dates come from Spanish chronicles and are approximate, and the empire fell to Spanish conquistadors after 1532.

title: Ewuare the Great expands Benin
summary: Oba Ewuare rebuilt Benin City and expanded the Edo kingdom of Benin into a major West African state famed for its brass and ivory art.
description: According to Edo tradition, Ewuare took the throne around 1440, rebuilt Benin City with broad streets, extended its vast system of earthen walls and moats, and strengthened royal power over the chiefs. The kingdom expanded through conquest and became a trading partner of the Portuguese after their arrival in the 1480s. Guilds of brass casters produced the plaques and heads now known as the Benin Bronzes, thousands of which were looted by a British expedition in 1897. Dates for the early obas rely on oral tradition.

title: King Sejong creates Hangul
summary: Joseon king Sejong the Great created Hangul, a phonetic alphabet designed so that ordinary Koreans could easily learn to read and write.
description: Korean had been written with Chinese characters, which few outside the educated elite could master. Sejong, fourth king of the Joseon dynasty founded in 1392, completed the new script in 1443 and promulgated it in 1446 in the Hunminjeongeum, 'the correct sounds for instructing the people'. Its consonant shapes represent the positions of the speech organs, and letters are grouped into syllable blocks. Resisted by many scholars, Hangul gained official status only in the late 19th century and is now the national script of both Koreas.

title: Fall of Constantinople
summary: Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople after a 53-day siege, ending the Byzantine Empire and making the city the Ottoman capital.
description: By 1453 the Byzantine Empire was reduced to little more than its capital, defended by about 7,000 men against an Ottoman army of perhaps 80,000. Mehmed II used huge cannon cast by the Hungarian engineer Orban to batter the Theodosian Walls and had ships hauled overland into the Golden Horn. The last emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, died in the final assault on 29 May. Constantinople, later known as Istanbul, became the capital of an expanding Ottoman Empire, and Greek scholars who moved to Italy contributed to the Renaissance; the date is often used to mark the end of the Middle Ages.

title: Gutenberg's printing press
summary: In Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg combined metal movable type, oil-based ink and a screw press to print his Bible, launching Europe's printing revolution.
description: Gutenberg developed a hand mould for casting uniform metal type in quantity from an alloy of lead, tin and antimony, an oil-based ink suited to metal, and a press adapted from those used for wine and paper. About 180 copies of his 42-line Latin Bible were printed around 1454–1455, of which 49 survive at least in part. By 1500 printing had spread to more than 250 European towns, producing perhaps 20 million volumes. Cheap printed books accelerated the Renaissance, the Protestant Reformation and the Scientific Revolution. Movable type had been invented earlier in China and Korea, but Gutenberg's system was especially well suited to alphabetic scripts.

title: Wars of the Roses
summary: Rival branches of England's royal house, Lancaster and York, fought a series of civil wars that ended with the Tudor dynasty on the throne.
description: Weak rule by Henry VI, defeat in France and factional rivalry led to armed conflict between the houses of Lancaster and York, beginning at St Albans in 1455. Edward IV of York won the throne in 1461, but power changed hands repeatedly. In 1485 Henry Tudor defeated and killed Richard III at Bosworth Field, and his marriage to Elizabeth of York united the rival claims; the Battle of Stoke in 1487 ended the main fighting. The name, taken from the red and white rose badges, was popularised much later, partly by Shakespeare and Walter Scott.

title: Sunni Ali builds the Songhai Empire
summary: From Gao on the Niger, Sunni Ali conquered Timbuktu and Djenné, beginning Songhai's rise into one of the largest empires in African history.
description: Songhai, long a tributary of Mali, expanded rapidly after Sunni Ali came to power around 1464; he took Timbuktu in 1468 and Djenné after a long siege. His successor Askia Muhammad (r. 1493–1528) extended the empire, reorganised its administration, made a pilgrimage to Mecca and promoted Islamic scholarship in Timbuktu. At its height Songhai controlled much of the Niger valley and the trans-Saharan trade. It fell after a Moroccan army equipped with firearms defeated it at Tondibi in 1591.

title: Fall of Granada ends the Reconquista
summary: Muhammad XII surrendered Granada, the last Muslim state in Iberia, to Ferdinand and Isabella, completing the Christian Reconquista.
description: Christian kingdoms had gradually pushed south since the 8th century, with decisive gains after the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 and the capture of Córdoba (1236) and Seville (1248). The Nasrid Emirate of Granada, builders of the Alhambra, survived as a tributary state until a ten-year war ended with its surrender. Within three months the Alhambra Decree ordered Spain's Jews to convert or leave, and Muslims were later forced to convert. Freed from the war, Isabella agreed that spring to sponsor Columbus's voyage.

title: Columbus reaches the Americas
summary: Christopher Columbus, sailing for Castile, made landfall in the Bahamas, beginning sustained contact between Europe and the Americas.
description: Columbus, a Genoese navigator, believed he could reach Asia by sailing west, having greatly underestimated the size of the Earth. With three ships he left Palos on 3 August 1492 and, after a stop in the Canary Islands, reached an island the Lucayan people called Guanahani, probably today's San Salvador. He went on to Cuba and Hispaniola, where he left the first Spanish settlement, before returning to Spain in 1493. His voyages began the Columbian exchange of crops, animals and diseases, the European colonisation of the Americas and a catastrophic decline of Indigenous populations.

title: Vasco da Gama reaches India by sea
summary: Portuguese navigator Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa to Calicut, opening a direct sea route between Europe and Asia.
description: Building on decades of Portuguese voyages down the African coast, including Bartolomeu Dias's rounding of the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, da Gama's fleet left Lisbon in July 1497. After stops on the Swahili coast, where a pilot hired at Malindi guided it across the Arabian Sea, it reached Calicut on the Malabar Coast in May 1498. The voyage cost many lives, mostly to scurvy, but the spices brought back were highly profitable. It opened Portuguese empire-building in the Indian Ocean and the era of direct European trade with Asia.

title: Phantom time hypothesis
summary: German writer Heribert Illig claimed that the years 614–911, including Charlemagne's entire reign, never happened and were invented by medieval rulers.
description: Proposed by Heribert Illig in 1991, the hypothesis asserts that Emperor Otto III, Pope Sylvester II and possibly the Byzantine emperor Constantine VII conspired to insert about 297 fictitious years into the calendar so that Otto would reign in the year 1000. Illig pointed to what he saw as a scarcity of archaeological evidence for the early Middle Ages, to the many forged medieval documents, and to the Gregorian calendar reform of 1582 correcting only ten days of drift rather than thirteen. On this view Charlemagne is a fictional figure and buildings such as the Palatine Chapel at Aachen are misdated.
mainstreamView: Historians and scientists reject the claim. Dendrochronology and radiocarbon dating give continuous, independently calibrated timelines through the 7th–10th centuries, and eclipses recorded by ancient and medieval observers match astronomical calculations only on the conventional chronology. Tang China, the Islamic caliphates and Byzantium kept independent records that synchronise with western dates, and the archaeology of these centuries, from Viking-Age sites to Carolingian buildings, is abundant. The ten-day Gregorian correction is fully explained because the reform realigned the calendar with the Council of Nicaea in 325, not with Julius Caesar's time.

title: Pope Joan, the legendary female pope
summary: Medieval chroniclers told of a woman who, disguised as a man, became pope in the 850s and was exposed when she gave birth during a procession in Rome.
description: The story first appears in the mid-13th century in the chronicle of the Dominican Jean de Mailly, and it spread widely through Martin of Opava's chronicle of popes and emperors in the 1270s. In Martin's version a learned woman from Mainz, disguised as a man, studied in Athens, was elected pope after Leo IV and reigned for more than two years, until she gave birth in a street between St Peter's and the Lateran and died. The tale was widely believed in the later Middle Ages, and a bust of her stood among the papal portraits in Siena Cathedral until about 1600. Protestant writers of the Reformation used it against the papacy, and a few modern authors have argued that a female pope really existed.
mainstreamView: Historians, Catholic and Protestant alike, regard Pope Joan as a legend. No source written before the mid-13th century mentions her, although the 9th-century papacy is well documented, and contemporary evidence, including a coin naming Benedict III with the emperor Lothair I, who died in September 855, shows that Benedict succeeded Leo IV within months, leaving no gap for another pontificate. The Huguenot scholar David Blondel argued in the 17th century that the story was fiction. Suggested origins include Roman folk tales, satire of the 10th-century papacy's domination by powerful Roman noblewomen, and anti-papal polemic.

title: New Chronology (Fomenko)
dateLabel: claims recorded history begins c. 1000 CE
summary: Mathematician Anatoly Fomenko claims ancient history is a duplicated fiction and that recorded civilisation essentially begins around 1000 CE.
description: Building on ideas of the revolutionary Nikolai Morozov, the Russian mathematician Anatoly Fomenko and colleagues argued from the 1980s that statistical similarities between lists of rulers show ancient Rome, Greece and Egypt to be phantom reflections of medieval events. In their reconstruction, history before roughly 1000 CE is largely fabricated, Jesus lived in the 11th or 12th century, and a vast 'Russian-Horde' empire ruled Eurasia until its memory was erased by later historians. The books have sold widely in Russia and have been promoted by public figures including the chess champion Garry Kasparov.
mainstreamView: Historians, archaeologists and scientists reject the New Chronology. Radiocarbon dating, dendrochronology, ice cores and ancient astronomical records independently confirm the conventional dating of ancient civilisations, as do coins, inscriptions and the independent chronologies of China, India and the Near East. Fomenko's statistical parallels depend on selective and manipulated data, and his redating of eclipses in classical sources rests on rejecting well-established identifications. Historians and scientists in Russia and elsewhere have published extensive critiques, and the theory is widely classed as pseudohistory.

title: Prince Madoc's claimed voyage to America
summary: A Welsh legend claims that Prince Madoc, a son of Owain Gwynedd, sailed west in 1170 and settled in America more than three centuries before Columbus.
description: According to the legend, Madoc left Wales during the quarrels among Owain Gwynedd's sons over the succession, sailed west and found a new land, then returned to lead more settlers there who never came back. The story was presented as history in Elizabethan England by John Dee and in Humphrey Llwyd's chronicle, published by David Powel in 1584, and Richard Hakluyt repeated it to support English claims to North America against Spain. From the 17th to the 19th century travellers reported encounters with Welsh-speaking 'Welsh Indians', and the Mandan of the upper Missouri were often named as Madoc's descendants. In 1953 the Daughters of the American Revolution placed a plaque at Fort Morgan on Mobile Bay, Alabama, stating that Madoc had landed there in 1170.
mainstreamView: Historians regard the voyage as legend. No contemporary source mentions it, the earliest possible allusions are in 15th-century Welsh poetry, and the story was built up in the 1580s largely to support English territorial claims. No Welsh artefacts, inscriptions or settlements have been found in the Americas, and accounts of 'Welsh Indians' did not survive investigation: the Welsh explorer John Evans, who went up the Missouri in 1795–1797 to find them, reported that the Mandan had no Welsh connection. The Mandan language belongs to the Siouan family and shows no Welsh influence.

title: Templar treasure on Oak Island
