summary: A popular theory holds that Knights Templar fleeing their suppression in 1307 carried treasure across the Atlantic and buried it on Oak Island, Nova Scotia.
description: On 13 October 1307 King Philip IV of France ordered the arrest of the Knights Templar, a wealthy military order, and the pope dissolved it in 1312. Legends grew that the order's treasure, or relics such as the Holy Grail, escaped on Templar ships from La Rochelle. Some authors claim these were later taken to North America, sometimes via a supposed 1398 voyage by the Scottish earl Henry Sinclair, and hidden in the 'Money Pit' on Oak Island, where treasure hunters have dug since about 1795. The idea has been popularised by books and television series.
mainstreamView: Historians find no evidence that the Templars had a hidden treasure fleet or crossed the Atlantic; the order's property was seized by the French crown or transferred to the Knights Hospitaller. The Henry Sinclair voyage rests on the Zeno narrative published in 1558, which most scholars regard as a fabrication. More than two centuries of digging on Oak Island have found no treasure, and geologists attribute features of the 'Money Pit' to natural sinkholes and tidal flooding in the island's soluble bedrock, compounded by earlier diggers' disturbance.

title: Kensington Runestone
summary: A stone found in Minnesota in 1898 bears a runic inscription claiming that Scandinavian explorers reached the area in 1362.
description: Swedish-American farmer Olof Ohman said he found the slab entangled in the roots of a tree near Kensington, Minnesota, in 1898. Its inscription describes 8 Götalanders and 22 Norwegians on an exploring journey west from Vinland who found ten of their companions dead. Supporters argue that it records a genuine 14th-century expedition, sometimes linked to a mission ordered by King Magnus Eriksson, and that its weathering is too advanced for a modern carving. The stone is displayed at the Runestone Museum in Alexandria, Minnesota.
mainstreamView: Runologists, linguists and historians overwhelmingly regard the stone as a 19th-century creation. Its language and rune forms match 19th-century Swedish dialects and later folk runic traditions rather than 14th-century Old Swedish or Old Norwegian, and it uses forms and numerals not found in medieval inscriptions. There is no archaeological evidence for Norse presence in the American Midwest; outside Greenland, the only confirmed Norse site in North America is L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, occupied around 1021.

title: Claimed Chinese discovery of America in 1421
summary: Retired naval officer Gavin Menzies claimed that Zheng He's fleets circled the globe and reached the Americas in 1421, decades before Columbus.
description: In his 2002 book '1421: The Year China Discovered the World', Gavin Menzies argued that squadrons of the Ming treasure fleet sailed around the world between 1421 and 1423, charting the Americas, Antarctica and Australia. He read early European maps, such as the 1424 Pizzigano chart, as showing Caribbean islands, including Puerto Rico, surveyed by the Chinese, and cited shipwrecks, plants, DNA and stone structures that he interpreted as Chinese. The book became a bestseller and was followed by sequels claiming Chinese influence on the Italian Renaissance.
wikipedia: 1421: The Year China Discovered the World
mainstreamView: Historians of China and of navigation reject the theory. Ming records of Zheng He's voyages describe destinations around the Indian Ocean as far as East Africa and say nothing of rounding Africa or crossing the Atlantic or Pacific, and no Chinese artefacts, wrecks or settlements of the period have been verified in the Americas. Menzies' map readings and physical evidence rest on speculative identifications; the islands on the Pizzigano chart are conventionally the legendary Antillia. Specialists in Ming history have published detailed critiques, and the book is widely regarded as pseudohistory.
